Ramnath

messages.subject: [GSoC student proposal] Reproducible working and developing environment for R (Rbundler)
messages.subject_clean: [GSoC student proposal] Reproducible working and developing environment for R (Rbundler)
messages.body_plain:
I know it's very late to bring a new proposal, but I just got the idea. The idea is simple, and the benefit shall be clear, for anyone who had ever struggled to resolve the broken dependences of some old code or code from other persons. Meanwhile, I'm contacting some experienced R developers in person, so hopefully, I can find some mentors in time. The details of proposal is following,

Summary: Reproducible working and developing environment for R (Rbundler)

Student: Chenliang Xu

Description: R handles dependences of packages properly and automatically, so we only need to call a few commands to installed all the required packages for a project. However, it’s quite often the dependences become broken after half year or so, because new versions of R and/or packages bring some conflicts. Furthermore, the claim “packages A, B, C must be installed” might actually mean “packages A, B, C  and some other packages on my current computer must be installed”. Without a clean prescription, it’s hard to reproduce the required working environment, not to mention the reproducible research result.

Inspired by Ruby/bundler <http://bundler.io/>, I would like to propose a method for reproducing working and developing environment for R reliably. By specifying the required packages and R version in a file in the project directory, a single call to command `Rbundler install` shall grab all the required packages, save them in cache and install them in local lib directory. It shall also create a snapshot file to describe the version of packages used. With the snapshot file and cached packages, the command `Rbundler restore snapshot_name` shall rebuild the same working environment exactly, on the same machine in the future or any other machines.

Target: A cross platform (Linux, Mac and Windows with proper developing tools installed) tool Rbundler supporting the following command,

Rbundler install  Download and cache the required packages, install them in local lib directory.

Rbundler restore snapshot_name Restore specific status of working environment on any computer.

Rbundler run Run R with local lib directory added to lib path.

Rbundler run --clean Run R in a clean environment, with only local lib directory in lib path.

Skills required: It’s more about the procedure of building, installing and loading R packages, rather than R programming.

Possible Side projects:  This section shows some potential benefits of this project. I may pursue them in the future, but they are not part of the Google summer of code project.

If the binary packages can be cached properly, we can prepare a clean environment with all the required dependencies, for testing and building R package easily and quickly.

Combining the lightweight Linux container docker <https://www.docker.io/> and Rbundler, we may easily deploy the production environment, including the external dependencies, to a Linux server or cloud.

By specifying the required packages and R version in a file in the project directory, a single call to command `Rbundler install` shall grab all the required packages, save them in cache and install them in local lib directory. It shall also create a snapshot file to describe the version of packages used. messages.body_plain:
Now that the student application process is open, I thought I would take
a moment to provide some information for both students and mentors.

As in prior years, we have project standards if you want your project to
get a slot.

Students:

The application template is here:
http://rwiki.sciviews.org/doku.php?id=developers:projects:student_app_template

All applications will be reviewed and ranked by all R mentors.

Applications that do not contain at least the minimum information in the
template *will not* get a slot.

The best applications run to several pages if printed, and show
considerable thought and planning.  The application process is longer
this year than it has been in some prior years, so this should not be a
problem.

Once your draft application has been submitted, you may receive comments
from other R mentors, either listed project mentor or others.  Please
respond to the comments promptly and completely.  Being non-responsive
before you've even been awarded a slot is not a good sign for the
success of your proposal.

Google's deadlines are firm, we don't control them, and can't allow late
submissions.

Mentors:

If you have not already done so, you need to sign in or register on
melange, fill out your profile and accept the terms, and initiate a
connection request to the 'R Project for Statistical Computing'. Please
make the org admin's lives easier and identify yourself and your project
idea page in your connection request.

Please make sure that your email (and ideally your melange link id) are
on your project idea page, we do ask the students to provide this
information in their applications.

If you and all your co-mentor(s) have the same university or company
affiliation, you need to find a mentor from some other institution.  We
try to spread things around a bit, and gather different perspectives.
If two of you are from the same institution, find a third co-mentor from
somewhere else.

If you are a first time GSoC mentor, I sincerely hope that you have an
experienced co-mentor.  GSoC is a lot of work, and we try to avoid
mentors disappearing or being overwhelmed in the middle of the summer.

If you don't have a co-mentor, you need to find one!  Projects will not
be approved with only one mentor, *especially* if you have no GSoC
experience (see above).

All mentors are encouraged to review all proposals that they feel
competent to comment on any aspect of.  Please help all our potential
students and mentors create better projects by asking questions and
making suggestions.  As in prior years, there are 'public' comments that
the student will see, and 'private' comments that only the other R
mentors will see for our internal discussion.

Please do not hesitate to email this list, me, or any of the other R
GSoC organization administrators with any questions.

Regards,

Brian

--

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am Prashant Kumar. I am interested in participating in Google Summer of Code 2014 by contributing to the R language project. I wish to develop a GMDH type Polynomial Neural Network package in R. I have used GMDH (Group Method of Data Handling) for my Master’s project in Geophysics. I have always been interested in machine learning and have used R in few of my geophysics related projects.

GMDH is a nonlinear regression method (Ivakhnenko, 1971) <http://www.gmdh.net/articles/history/polynomial.pdf> but also shares the characteristics of both unsupervised and supervised artificial neural networks. GMDH has the advantage of automatically determining the best network structure and number of nodes without overtraining the data. GMDH methods are used in fields such as biomedical modeling, econometric forecasting, environmental systems.

It would be great if you could guide me further.

Regards

Sincerely

Prashant Kumar

> Now that the student application process is open, I thought I would take

>
> As in prior years, we have project standards if you want your project to
> get a slot.
>
> Students:
>
> The application template is here:
> http://rwiki.sciviews.org/doku.php?id=developers:projects:student_app_template
>
> All applications will be reviewed and ranked by all R mentors.
>
> Applications that do not contain at least the minimum information in the
> template *will not* get a slot.
>
> The best applications run to several pages if printed, and show
> considerable thought and planning.  The application process is longer
> this year than it has been in some prior years, so this should not be a
> problem.
>
> Once your draft application has been submitted, you may receive comments
> from other R mentors, either listed project mentor or others.  Please
> respond to the comments promptly and completely.  Being non-responsive
> before you've even been awarded a slot is not a good sign for the
> success of your proposal.
>
> Google's deadlines are firm, we don't control them, and can't allow late
> submissions.
>
> Mentors:
>
> If you have not already done so, you need to sign in or register on
> melange, fill out your profile and accept the terms, and initiate a
> connection request to the 'R Project for Statistical Computing'. Please
> make the org admin's lives easier and identify yourself and your project
> idea page in your connection request.
>
> Please make sure that your email (and ideally your melange link id) are
> on your project idea page, we do ask the students to provide this
> information in their applications.
>
> If you and all your co-mentor(s) have the same university or company
> affiliation, you need to find a mentor from some other institution.  We
> try to spread things around a bit, and gather different perspectives.
> If two of you are from the same institution, find a third co-mentor from
> somewhere else.
>
> If you are a first time GSoC mentor, I sincerely hope that you have an
> experienced co-mentor.  GSoC is a lot of work, and we try to avoid
> mentors disappearing or being overwhelmed in the middle of the summer.
>
> If you don't have a co-mentor, you need to find one!  Projects will not
> be approved with only one mentor, *especially* if you have no GSoC
> experience (see above).
>
> All mentors are encouraged to review all proposals that they feel
> competent to comment on any aspect of.  Please help all our potential
> students and mentors create better projects by asking questions and
> making suggestions.  As in prior years, there are 'public' comments that
> the student will see, and 'private' comments that only the other R
> mentors will see for our internal discussion.
>
> Please do not hesitate to email this list, me, or any of the other R
> GSoC organization administrators with any questions.
>
> Regards,
>
> Brian
